# 2.2 Example 1

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

As we learned in the last chapter, the first thing we want to do when
faced with a passage is ask ourselves, **"What is this passage doing? Is
it trying to convince us that something is true?"**

So let's begin this chapter by asking that question of this text:

> "Censorship is the practice of suppressing claims and images which are
> considered to be obscene, dangerous, offensive or otherwise
> objectionable. Governments, religious organizations, media outlets,
> and even educational institutions can engage in censorship, which is
> essential for a well-run society."

It might be tempting to say, "This contains an argument because I could
argue with it." After all, it's pretty controversial to say that
censorship is essential for a well-run society! But remember,
"argument," for us, doesn't mean "dispute." The issue at hand isn't how
provocative a passage might be. The only question is whether or not the
passage is trying to convince us of something (controversial or not) by
advancing reasons to support it. In this case, it doesn't seem to me
that the passage *is* trying to convince us something is true, so I'll
say that this passage doesn't contain an argument.

("Which is" might look like an inference indicator expression, but it
isn't. It's basically short for the sentence "Censorship is essential
for a well-run society." In fact, there are no inference indicator
expressions in this passage, and for now this can be a clue that there's
no argument here. Later on, though, we'll see arguments that don't
contain inference indicator expressions, so we shouldn't get in the
habit of relying too heavily on that.)

## Summary of Example 1

 

We saw that the following passage doesn't convey an argument because it
isn't trying to convince us that something is true, even though it might
be controversial.

> "Censorship is the practice of suppressing claims and images which are
> considered to be obscene, dangerous, offensive or otherwise
> objectionable. Governments, religious organizations, media outlets,
> and even educational institutions can engage in censorship, which is
> essential for a well-run society."
